questions.q: You check an A/B test's p-value every day and stop as soon as it drops below 0.05. What is the problem?
options: Nothing; more looks always make the result more reliable
Each look is another chance for noise to cross the threshold, so the false positive rate climbs well above 5 percent
The p-value can only be computed once
It lowers the effect size
questions.explain: In the lesson's simulation of an A/A test, one planned look gave about 4 percent significant, while ten looks gave about 20 percent.

questions.q: Treatment beats control in both the desktop and mobile segments, but loses overall. What best explains this?
options: Simpson's paradox: the treatment group had a very different mix of segments, dominated by low-converting mobile users
The p-value is wrong
Regression to the mean
The sample size was too large
questions.explain: When groups have different segment mixes, the aggregated rate can reverse the within-segment trend.

questions.q: A company picks its 100 top-performing stores this year and gives them a training program. Next year they improve less, but they still beat average. What is a likely reason to be careful about crediting the program?
options: The stores got worse because of the program
Training programs never work
The top stores' scores were partly luck, so they tend to fall back toward average even without intervention
The average of the whole company must have risen
questions.explain: Selecting extremes selects partly on luck. Compare with a control group selected the same way to isolate the program's effect.

questions.q: You test 20 independent metrics at alpha 0.05 when no real effects exist. About how likely is at least one 'significant' result?
options: 5 percent
About 20 percent
About 50 percent
About 64 percent
questions.explain: The chance is 1 minus 0.95 to the 20th power, about 0.64. Choose a primary metric in advance or correct for multiple comparisons.

questions.q: Which of these is a good habit to protect an analysis from the pitfalls in this lesson?
options: Wait to choose your primary metric until after you have seen which one looks best
Fix the metric, sample size, and stopping rule up front, and report effect size with a confidence interval
Analyze only the customers who stayed, since they have complete data
Stop the experiment as soon as p is below 0.05
questions.explain: Deciding the protocol before seeing outcomes and reporting effect sizes with intervals guards against peeking, metric-fishing, and overreading tiny effects.
